processing: Medium oxidation, strip-rolled and charcoal roasted medium to medium-heavy, usually in two passes with a rest between them.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May, as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Tight, dark brown twisted strips of medium size with a warm roasted-fruit smell.
appearance_wet: Thick olive-brown leaves with even red edges, firm and glossy.
taste_profile: A quieter Da Hong Pao: toasted grain, dried plum and a faint orchid note on a thick, smooth body, with a long, cooling mineral aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, a gaiwan or a zisha pot. Decant fully each time; it holds eight infusions easily and the sweetness builds from the fourth.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the year stated. Medium-roasted Bei Dou drinks well on release and improves for a year or two; it keeps three to five years sealed and dry and is sometimes re-roasted and sold aged.
description:
Bei Dou is a cultivar long sold as pure Da Hong Pao, with an argued-over pedigree. It makes a classic, balanced rock tea with roast, dried fruit and a long mineral finish, closer to the textbook idea of Da Hong Pao than most blends that carry that name.

The plant is linked to the Wuyi tea scientist Yao Yueming, who in the 1960s took cuttings from bushes at Bei Dou Peak, Jiulongke and Huoyan Peak that were reputed to descend from the Da Hong Pao line, and the name Bei Dou No. 1 dates from that work. For decades much of the commercial Da Hong Pao was in fact Bei Dou. Genetic testing later found it distinct from the Jiulongke mother trees and pointed to Qi Dan as the match, and in 2012 Qi Dan was recognised as the true Da Hong Pao, so today Bei Dou is usually sold under its own name and prized on its own merits.

It is made in the standard Wuyi way, picked mature in spring, shaken through the night, rolled and charcoal roasted, and most makers give it a medium to medium-heavy roast. The leaf has enough thickness to carry that: the cup is smooth, with toasted grain and dried plum first, a hint of orchid in the middle steeps and a mineral, slightly cooling finish that lingers.

Brew it hot and quick in a well-filled gaiwan or a zisha pot, and expect it to peak around the third and fourth steeps. It is a steady, well-mannered tea rather than a showy one, which is exactly why blenders like it and why it suits daily drinking.

Bei Dou is widely planted inside and outside the scenic area, so prices vary a lot; ask where it grew and in which year it was roasted. Tasting it side by side with Qi Dan is the most instructive thing you can do with it, because that shows the old idea of Da Hong Pao next to the officially recognised one.
history:
Bei Dou's story is tied to Yao Yueming (1932 to 2006), an authority on Wuyi tea. According to one English-language tea article, he helped survey Wuyi's famous varieties in 1953 to 1955 and in the 1960s took ten cuttings from Bei Dou Peak, Jiulongke and Huoyan Peak, of which four survived. The same article says the name Bei Dou No. 1 came from his teacher Wu Juenong and was used during the Cultural Revolution to protect the plants, and that the Da Hong Pao name came back afterwards, which is how the idea that Bei Dou was Da Hong Pao spread.

Genetic testing undid that idea. A Chinese article reports a 2009 analysis in which Bei Dou stood at a genetic distance from the Da Hong Pao mother trees, while Qi Dan matched trees 2 and 6. In 2012 the Fujian variety committee recognised Qi Dan as the true Da Hong Pao, and Bei Dou is now better treated as a cultivar in its own right. The English article dates a test to the 1980s and says Yao's cuttings were not included, so parts of this record remain unclear.
